mcqs.stem: Q3.1. Which of the following Boolean expressions represents the OR operation?
rationales: A · B represents the AND operation, not OR.
A + B is the Boolean notation for OR.
A̅ represents the complement of A, or NOT A.
A ⊕ B represents exclusive OR, which is different from ordinary OR.

mcqs.stem: Q3.2. What is the dual of the Boolean expression A · 0 = 0?
rationales: Interchanging · with + and 0 with 1 gives A + 1 = 1.
This is a valid Boolean identity, but it is not the dual of the given expression.
This is a valid Boolean identity, but it is not the dual of the given expression.
This repeats the original expression instead of forming its dual.

mcqs.stem: Q3.3. Which logic gate outputs true only if both inputs are true?
rationales: An OR gate outputs true when at least one input is true.
An AND gate outputs true only when both inputs are true.
An XOR gate outputs true when its inputs are different.
A NOT gate has one input and reverses its value.

mcqs.stem: Q3.4. In a half-adder circuit, the carry is generated by which operation?
rationales: XOR generates the sum output of a half-adder.
AND generates the carry when both input bits are 1.
OR is not the half-adder carry operation.
NOT reverses a value and does not generate the half-adder carry.

written.text: Q3.1. Define a Boolean function and give an example.
written.finalAnswer: A Boolean function maps one or more binary inputs to a binary output; for example, F(A, B) = A + B.

rubric.why: The definition must show that a Boolean function relates binary inputs to an output.
rubric.how: State that it maps binary input values to a binary output.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.how: Write a correct expression, such as F(A, B) = A + B.

modelAnswer: A Boolean function maps one or more binary inputs to a binary output.
For example, F(A, B) = A + B.

written.text: Q3.2. What is the significance of the truth table in digital logic?
written.finalAnswer: A truth table lists every possible input combination and the corresponding output of a logic function.

rubric.why: A truth table must cover the full set of possible inputs.
rubric.how: Say that every possible input combination is included.

rubric.why: The table is useful because it shows the output for each input combination.
rubric.how: Explain that it records the corresponding output of the logic function.

modelAnswer: A truth table lists every possible input combination.
It shows the corresponding output of a logic function for each combination.

written.text: Q3.3. Explain the difference between analog and digital signals.
written.finalAnswer: An analog signal varies continuously, while a digital signal has distinct discrete values, usually 0 and 1.

rubric.why: Continuity is the key feature distinguishing an analog signal.
rubric.how: State that it varies continuously.

rubric.why: Digital signals use distinct values rather than a continuous range.
rubric.how: State that it has discrete values, usually 0 and 1.

modelAnswer: An analog signal varies continuously.
A digital signal has distinct discrete values, usually 0 and 1.

written.text: Q3.4. Describe the function of a NOT gate with its truth table.
written.finalAnswer: A NOT gate reverses its input: 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0.

rubric.why: The function of a NOT gate is to produce the complement of its input.
rubric.how: State that it reverses or complements its input.

rubric.why: The truth table must show both possible input-output pairs.
rubric.how: Show input 0 gives output 1 and input 1 gives output 0.

modelAnswer: A NOT gate gives the complement of its input.
Input A | Output A̅

written.text: Q3.5. What is the purpose of a Karnaugh map in simplifying Boolean expressions?
written.finalAnswer: A Karnaugh map groups adjacent 1s to obtain a simpler Boolean expression with fewer terms or variables.

rubric.why: Grouping adjacent cells is the central Karnaugh map method.
rubric.how: State that adjacent 1s are grouped.

rubric.why: The purpose of grouping is to reduce the Boolean expression.
rubric.how: Explain that the groups produce a simpler expression.

modelAnswer: A Karnaugh map groups adjacent 1s.
The groups give a simpler Boolean expression with fewer terms or variables.

written.text: Q3.1. Explain the usage of Boolean functions in computers.
written.finalAnswer: Boolean functions describe how binary inputs are processed to produce binary outputs and are used to design and control computer logic circuits.

rubric.why: Boolean functions operate on binary values.
rubric.how: Explain that their inputs and outputs use 0 and 1.

rubric.why: Boolean operations are implemented by logic gates.
rubric.how: Give gates such as AND, OR, and NOT as implementations.

rubric.why: The answer must explain where these functions are used.
rubric.how: State that they describe or control computer logic circuits.

rubric.why: This states the practical role of Boolean functions in processing and decision-making.
rubric.how: Explain that they determine outputs from input conditions.

modelAnswer: Computers process information in binary form, using 0 and 1.
A Boolean function describes the relationship between binary inputs and a binary output.
The basic Boolean operations are implemented by logic gates such as AND, OR, and NOT.
These gates are combined to form logic circuits.
Boolean functions therefore describe how a circuit responds to its input conditions.
They are used in computer circuits for operations such as making decisions and processing data.

written.text: Q3.2. Describe how to construct a truth table for a Boolean expression with an example.
written.finalAnswer: For F = A + B, list the four input pairs and evaluate OR for each: 00 → 0, 01 → 1, 10 → 1, 11 → 1.

rubric.why: A truth table must include every possible input combination.
rubric.how: For two inputs, list 00, 01, 10, and 11.

rubric.why: The example expression and its operation must be identified.
rubric.how: Use F = A + B and identify + as OR.

rubric.why: Correctly evaluating rows shows how the expression is applied.
rubric.how: For OR, 00 gives 0 and 01 gives 1.

rubric.why: The remaining rows complete the truth table and its final result.
rubric.how: For OR, 10 and 11 both give 1.

modelAnswer: Example: Construct a truth table for F = A + B.
There are two inputs, so list all four possible input combinations.
Evaluate F using the OR operation for each combination.
A | B | F = A + B

written.text: Q3.3. Describe the concept of duality in Boolean algebra and provide an example to illustrate it.
written.finalAnswer: To form the dual, interchange + with · and 0 with 1; for example, the dual of A · 0 = 0 is A + 1 = 1.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the Boolean algebra principle being described.
rubric.how: Name duality and explain that an expression is changed by prescribed substitutions.

rubric.why: The two operators must be interchanged to form the dual.
rubric.how: Replace + by · and · by +.

rubric.why: The constants must also be interchanged.
rubric.how: Replace 0 by 1 and 1 by 0.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates how duality is applied.
rubric.description: Give the example and its dual.
rubric.how: Show that A · 0 = 0 has dual A + 1 = 1.

modelAnswer: Duality is a principle of Boolean algebra used to form the dual of an expression.
Interchange + and · in the expression.
Also interchange 0 and 1.
For example, start with A · 0 = 0.
Interchanging · with + and 0 with 1 gives A + 1 = 1.
Therefore, the dual of A · 0 = 0 is A + 1 = 1.

written.text: Q3.4. Compare and contrast half-adders and full-adders, including their truth tables, Boolean expressions, and circuit diagrams.
written.finalAnswer: A half-adder adds two bits with Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B; a full-adder adds A, B, and Cin with Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = A · B + A · Cin + B · Cin.

rubric.why: The half-adder's input limitation distinguishes it from a full-adder.
rubric.how: State that it adds two input bits and has no carry input.

rubric.why: A full-adder must include the carry from the previous bit position.
rubric.how: State that it adds A, B, and Cin.

rubric.why: These are the half-adder sum and carry expressions.
rubric.how: Write Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B.

rubric.why: The full-adder equations and its truth-table or circuit description complete the comparison.
rubric.how: Write the full-adder expressions and show its truth table or circuit construction.

modelAnswer: A half-adder adds two input bits, A and B. It has no carry input.
Half-adder expressions: Sum = A ⊕ B; Carry = A · B.
A | B | Sum | Carry
Circuit: connect A and B to an XOR gate for Sum and to an AND gate for Carry.
A full-adder adds A, B, and an input carry Cin.
Full-adder expressions: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin; Cout = A · B + A · Cin + B · Cin.
A | B | Cin | Sum | Cout
Circuit: use two half-adders in series to form the sum, then OR their carry outputs to form Cout.

written.text: Q3.5. How do Karnaugh maps simplify Boolean expressions? Provide a detailed example with steps.
written.finalAnswer: A Karnaugh map simplifies an expression by grouping adjacent 1s; for F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7), the simplified result is F = C.

rubric.why: The method being used must be identified.
rubric.how: Name the Karnaugh map method.

rubric.why: Grouping adjacent 1-cells is the central simplification step.
rubric.how: Group adjacent 1s in powers of two where possible.

rubric.why: A valid worked example and its minterms make the simplification steps checkable.
rubric.how: Use the stated function and place its 1s in the map.

rubric.why: The final simplified expression is the result of the grouping.
rubric.how: State F = C.

modelAnswer: A Karnaugh map places the function values in cells arranged so adjacent cells differ in one variable.
Example: simplify F(A, B, C) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7).
Place 1s in cells 1, 3, 5, and 7; place 0s in the other cells.
These four 1-cells form one group of four adjacent cells.
In the group, A and B change while C remains 1.
The changing variables A and B are eliminated.
Therefore, the simplified expression is F = C.

written.text: Q3.6. Design a 4-bit binary adder using both half-adders and full-adders. Explain each step with truth tables, Boolean expressions, and circuit diagrams.
written.finalAnswer: Use a half-adder for the least significant bits and three full-adders for the remaining bit positions; connect each carry output to the next stage's carry input.

rubric.why: The first stage adds the least significant bits when there is no initial carry.
rubric.how: Use a half-adder for bit 0.

rubric.why: The higher stages must add the incoming carry.
rubric.how: Use full-adders for bits 1, 2, and 3.

rubric.why: The half-adder equations define the first stage outputs.
rubric.how: Write its sum and carry expressions.

rubric.why: The full-adder equations and carry connections show how the four stages work together.
rubric.how: Write its sum and carry expressions and connect each Cout to the next Cin.

modelAnswer: Let the two 4-bit numbers be A3A2A1A0 and B3B2B1B0.
Stage 0: connect A0 and B0 to a half-adder.
Stages 1, 2, and 3: use one full-adder at each bit position.
For each full-adder, Si = Ai ⊕ Bi ⊕ Ci.
For each full-adder, Ci+1 = Ai · Bi + Ai · Ci + Bi · Ci.
Connect C1 from stage 0 to the carry input of stage 1.
Connect each later carry output to the next full-adder carry input.
The outputs are S3S2S1S0 and the final carry C4.
Circuit connection: HA(A0, B0) → FA(A1, B1, C1) → FA(A2, B2, C2) → FA(A3, B3, C3).
The half-adder truth table is 00→Sum 0, Carry 0; 01→1, 0; 10→1, 0; 11→0, 1.
For each full-adder, the output truth table is: 000→00; 001→10; 010→10; 011→01; 100→10; 101→01; 110→01; 111→11, where each pair is Sum, Carry.

written.text: Q3.7. Simplify the following Boolean function using Boolean algebra rules: F (A, B) = A · B + A · B̅

rubric.why: Factoring the common term is the key first algebra step.
rubric.how: Write A · B + A · B̅ = A · (B + B̅).

rubric.why: A variable ORed with its complement equals 1.
rubric.how: Use B + B̅ = 1.

rubric.why: The identity law reduces the remaining product.
rubric.how: Use A · 1 = A.

rubric.why: The simplified final expression must be stated.
rubric.how: State F(A, B) = A.

modelAnswer: F(A, B) = A · B + A · B̅
F(A, B) = A · (B + B̅)
F(A, B) = A · 1
F(A, B) = A

written.text: Q3.8. Use De Morgan's laws to simplify the following function: F (A, B, C) = \overline{A + B} + \overline{AC}

rubric.why: De Morgan's law changes the complement of a sum into the product of the complements.
rubric.how: Use overline(A + B) = A̅ · B̅.

rubric.why: De Morgan's law changes the complement of a product into the sum of the complements.
rubric.how: Use overline(A · C) = A̅ + C̅.

rubric.why: Combining both expansions gives the expression to simplify.
rubric.how: Substitute both De Morgan expansions into F.

rubric.why: Absorption removes the redundant product term.
rubric.how: Use X + X · Y = X to state F = A̅ + C̅.

modelAnswer: F(A, B, C) = overline(A + B) + overline(A · C)
By De Morgan's law, overline(A + B) = A̅ · B̅.
By De Morgan's law, overline(A · C) = A̅ + C̅.
F(A, B, C) = A̅ · B̅ + A̅ + C̅
Using X + X · Y = X, A̅ + A̅ · B̅ = A̅.
Therefore, F(A, B, C) = A̅ + C̅.

written.text: Q3.9. Simplify the following expressions (a) \overline{A + B} · (A + B)

rubric.why: Recognising a quantity and its complement identifies the applicable law.
rubric.description: Identify the expression and its complement.
rubric.how: Let X = A + B, so the expression is X̅ · X.

rubric.why: A quantity ANDed with its complement is 0.
rubric.how: Use X̅ · X = 0.

rubric.why: The final simplified value is required.
rubric.how: State the expression equals 0.

modelAnswer: overline(A + B) · (A + B)
Let X = A + B.
The expression is X̅ · X.
By the complement law, X̅ · X = 0.
Answer: 0

written.text: Q3.9. Simplify the following expressions (b) (A + B̅) · (A + B)

rubric.why: The expression must be correctly brought into a usable form.
rubric.how: Copy the two factors accurately.

rubric.why: The identity (X + Y)(X + Z) = X + YZ reduces the product.
rubric.how: Reduce to A + B̅ · B.

rubric.why: A variable multiplied by its complement equals 0.
rubric.how: Use B̅ · B = 0.

rubric.why: The result after applying the identity law is the final simplified expression.
rubric.how: State A + 0 = A.

modelAnswer: = A

written.text: Q3.9. Simplify the following expressions (c) A + A̅ · (B̅ + C)

rubric.why: The expression must be correctly identified before applying Boolean laws.
rubric.how: Copy the expression accurately.

rubric.why: Distributing the product across the sum makes absorption clear.
rubric.how: Use A̅ · (B̅ + C) = A̅ · B̅ + A̅ · C.

rubric.why: Absorption simplifies A + A̅ · B̅ to A + B̅.
rubric.how: Use X + X̅Y = X + Y.

rubric.why: The final expression must be stated in simplified form.
rubric.how: State A + B̅ + C.

modelAnswer: = A + B̅ + A̅ · C
= A + B̅ + C

written.text: Q3.9. Simplify the following expressions (d) \overline{A · B} + A · B̅

rubric.why: De Morgan's law correctly expands the complemented product.
rubric.how: Change overline(A · B) into A̅ + B̅.

rubric.why: The expansion must be combined with the remaining term.
rubric.how: Substitute the expansion into the expression.

rubric.why: The extra product term is absorbed by the existing sum.
rubric.how: Use A̅ + A · B̅ = A̅ + B̅.

rubric.why: The simplified final expression must be stated.
rubric.how: State A̅ + B̅.

modelAnswer: overline(A · B) + A · B̅
Answer: A̅ + B̅

written.text: Q3.9. Simplify the following expressions (e) (A · B) + (A̅ · B̅)

rubric.why: The original expression must be accurately represented.
rubric.how: Keep both product terms and their complements correctly placed.

rubric.why: Checking input pairs shows when the function is 1 and confirms its meaning.
rubric.how: State that it is 1 when A and B are equal.

rubric.why: The expression is the equivalence (XNOR) function.
rubric.how: Identify it as XNOR or equivalence.

rubric.why: This is already the simplified sum-of-products form.
rubric.how: State the expression remains A · B + A̅ · B̅.

modelAnswer: The first product is 1 when A = 1 and B = 1.
The second product is 1 when A = 0 and B = 0.
Thus, the function is 1 when A and B are equal.
This is the XNOR (equivalence) function.
The simplified expression is A · B + A̅ · B̅.

explain.title: Binary signals and Boolean functions
explain.body: Digital systems use binary values, 0 and 1. A Boolean function describes how input values determine an output, for example F(A, B) = A + B.

explain.title: Logic gates and truth tables
explain.body: AND, OR, and NOT gates carry out Boolean operations. A truth table lists every possible input combination and the output for each one.

explain.title: Boolean laws and duality
explain.body: Boolean laws help simplify expressions. To form a dual, interchange + and ·, and interchange 0 and 1; for example, the dual of A · 0 = 0 is A + 1 = 1.

explain.title: Adders
explain.body: A half-adder adds two bits: Sum = A ⊕ B and Carry = A · B. A full-adder also adds an input carry: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin and Cout = A · B + A · Cin + B · Cin.

explain.title: Karnaugh maps
explain.body: A Karnaugh map arranges output values so adjacent 1s can be grouped. Each larger valid group can remove variables and produce a simpler expression.

mistakes: Do not confuse Boolean OR (+) with arithmetic addition; it outputs 1 if at least one input is 1.
Do not use XOR as a synonym for OR: XOR outputs 1 only when its inputs differ.
When forming a dual, interchange both operators (+ and ·) and constants (0 and 1).
Do not omit input combinations from a truth table.
In a half-adder, the carry is A · B and the sum is A ⊕ B; do not swap them.
When simplifying, keep complements attached to the correct variables and show each law-based step.
